question: What is the main job of the mucociliary escalator in our airways?

options.A: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide in the tiny air sacs
options.B: Making surfactant to keep the lungs from collapsing
options.C: Filtering big dust bits right inside the nose
options.D: Sweeping trapped dirt and mucus upward toward the throat

explanation: Think of the mucociliary escalator like a tiny conveyor belt in your respiratory tract. It uses beating hair-like cilia and mucus to push dust and germs up to your throat so you can swallow or cough them out cleanly!

question: Which nursing action is a great example of secondary prevention for respiratory health?

options.A: Running a community talk on the dangers of smoking
options.B: Teaching an asthma patient how to use their inhaler properly
options.C: Giving the yearly flu shot to a healthy adult
options.D: Screening high-risk factory workers with routine breathing tests

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about early detection! Screening tests help catch signs of trouble early, before a patient even notices symptoms.

question: What is the single biggest preventable cause of chronic lung disease (COPD) worldwide?
explanation: Tobacco smoke is tough on the airways and air sacs over time. Because people can choose to avoid or quit it, it stands out as the number one preventable cause of COPD globally.

question: A patient living in a rural home with poor kitchen ventilation uses wood for daily cooking and now has a lasting cough. What is the best primary prevention advice?

options.A: Give them a course of strong oral antibiotics right away
options.B: Recommend using a quick-relief rescue inhaler every day
options.C: Order a chest X-ray to check for tuberculosis
options.D: Advise the family to switch to cleaner cooking fuel and improve kitchen airflow

explanation: Primary prevention stops the problem before it starts or worsens. Fixing indoor smoke exposure removes the root environmental trigger keeping that cough going!

question: Why do people need to take the influenza vaccine every single year?

options.A: The government needs yearly numbers for health records
options.B: The vaccine turns toxic if stored for more than a year
options.C: The flu virus mutates and changes its shape from year to year
options.D: Immunity from last year's shot completely disappears in six months

explanation: Flu viruses are clever changelings! They undergo constant changes (antigenic drift), so scientists update the vaccine annually to match whatever strain is currently spreading.

question: Which group of people benefits the most from herd immunity against respiratory infections?

options.A: Young adults working in busy office buildings
options.B: Older adults who get their flu shots on time
options.C: People who are too young or have weak immune systems to get vaccines

explanation: Herd immunity acts like a protective shield. When most of the community is vaccinated, it stops the germ from spreading to vulnerable people who cannot take vaccines themselves.

question: In occupational health, what is the FIRST and best line of defense against workplace air hazards?

options.A: Putting up exhaust fans in the work area
options.B: Giving workers certified face masks or respirators
options.C: Rotating shifts so workers spend less time near the hazard
options.D: Completely removing or replacing the dangerous material

explanation: Elimination and substitution are top priorities in safety. If you get rid of the hazard entirely, nobody has to rely on masks or fans to stay safe!

question: Which of these is a classic lung disease caused by breathing in mineral dust at work?
explanation: Silicosis happens when workers breathe in tiny crystalline silica dust, often found in mining, construction, or masonry jobs.

question: What is the main reason for doing screening spirometry on healthy workers who are at high risk?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen is floating in the blood
options.B: To cure existing chronic lung disease
options.C: To catch early breathing trouble before any symptoms show up
options.D: To find out which exact bacteria is causing an infection

explanation: Spirometry is a breathing test that can spot small changes in lung function long before a worker starts feeling short of breath.

question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of secondary prevention in respiratory health?

options.A: Finding small pulmonary nodules on routine diagnostic imaging
options.B: Reversing the genetic mutations that cause inherited lung disorders
options.C: Identifying early airway obstruction using breathing tests
options.D: Catching latent infections before they become active and contagious

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and treatment of existing disease, not genetic modification or primary prevention of DNA mutations. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention for someone living with COPD?

options.A: Slowing down the disease and preventing troublesome complications
options.B: Preventing airway inflammation back when they were a child
options.C: Screening healthy family members for hidden lung issues
options.D: Completely curing the permanent damage in the air sacs

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a chronic illness is already present. The aim is to help the patient manage symptoms, stay active, and avoid severe flare-ups.

question: What activities are normally included in a pulmonary rehabilitation program?

options.A: Supervised exercise training and breathing exercises
options.C: Long-term isolation so the patient avoids all outside air
options.D: Surgical replacement of damaged lung tissue

explanation: Pulmonary rehab is wonderful for chronic lung patients! It combines guided physical activity and breathing techniques to help them breathe easier and build stamina.

question: How does a nurse best show public health advocacy regarding breathing disorders?

options.A: Doing deep lung biopsies in local health clinics
options.B: Isolating every single person with a seasonal flu
options.C: Supporting policies that cut down air pollution and tobacco use
options.D: Prescribing strong bronchodilators to people in the neighborhood

explanation: Advocacy goes beyond the hospital bedside. Nurses advocate by supporting healthier environments, clean air policies, and community tobacco control.

question: A nurse is teaching an asthma patient how to use an inhaler. What is the best way to make sure the teaching worked?

options.A: Explaining the complex chemistry of the aerosol drug
options.B: Giving the patient a textbook chapter to read at home
options.C: Telling a family member to always give the medicine for them
options.D: Demonstrating the technique and asking the patient to show it back

explanation: Return demonstration is the gold standard of patient education! It lets you watch the patient do it themselves so you know they truly understand the steps.
